name: Treaty with the Kickapoo, 1832
aka: Treaty of Castor Hill with the Kickapoo, October 24, 1832
promises: A country south-west of the Missouri River as the Kickapoo's permanent place of residence 'as long as they remain a tribe' (Article 2; the supplemental article fixed a reservation in north-east Kansas).
$18,000 for one year, $12,000 of it applied to the tribe's debts, then $5,000 a year for nineteen years (Articles 3 and 4).
$1,000 a year for five years for a blacksmith, $3,700 for a mill and a church, $500 a year for ten years for a school, and $3,000 for farming tools (Articles 5 to 8).

breaches.what: The Kickapoo claimed before the Indian Claims Commission that they ceded their 1,868,500-acre Missouri tract under this treaty for an unconscionable consideration, about $143,000 in payments and a 768,000-acre reservation in Kansas. The claim was settled for a net final judgment of $540,000, approved by both Kickapoo tribes, without a ruling on the merits.

landTaken: The Missouri tract of 1,868,500 acres the Kickapoo had received under the treaty of 19 July 1820 (Royce Area 179) (Docket 193 findings, 1968).
compensation: Payments and expenditures said to amount to $143,000 plus a Kansas reservation of 768,000 acres. Settlement judgment of $540,000 in 1968, net of the treaty consideration.
today: The 'permanent' Kansas reservation was itself reduced by the treaty of 18 May 1854, when 618,000 acres were ceded and 150,000 kept; the Commission later awarded a net $771,441.26 for that cession (Docket 316, 1967).

nationVoice.summary: Chairman Lester Randall told the Senate in 2018 that the Tribe has lived in northeast Kansas since the 1832 Treaty of Castor Hill, that this treaty gives it senior water rights reserving enough of the Delaware River to make the reservation a permanent homeland, and that later cessions in 1854 and 1862, the second opposed by the Tribe, cut the land down and opened it to allotment and homesteading.

openQuestions: The settlement made no finding of unconscionable consideration, so this treaty is shown as contested. The 1854 reduction of the Kansas reservation may support a breach of the Article 2 'permanent residence' promise, but the 1854 cession was by treaty and is a separate queue entry (kappler-642).
The Docket 316 findings give the Kansas reservation as 765,000 acres; the Docket 193 findings give 768,000.
A web search found no Kickapoo tribal page on this treaty; a nation statement is still wanted.
